definition: Rebuttal means an argument made to counter or disprove a claim.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word rebuttal. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know rebuttal should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The debate coach grades every rebuttal on one question: did it answer the argument actually made, or the one you wish they'd made?
A denial is weaker than a rebuttal — it rejects the claim flatly but brings no reasons to the table.
A refutation goes further than a rebuttal: a rebuttal argues against the claim, while a refutation finishes it, proving the thing false outright.

A counterargument is the case built against a claim — the reasons and evidence assembled on the other side, wherever and whenever they appear. A rebuttal is that case deployed as a reply: it answers an argument someone actually made, inside the exchange where they made it. Every rebuttal contains a counterargument; only the answering ones are rebuttals.

A rejoinder is a sharp answering reply in an exchange — quick, pointed, and often more about wit than proof. A rebuttal carries the heavier duty: it has to take the claim apart with reasons or evidence. A rejoinder can win the laugh; a rebuttal has to win the point.

Rebuttal means an argument made to counter or disprove a claim.
The star witness swore the warehouse stood empty by six.

The defense's rebuttal needed no stack of exhibits — only the courthouse clock and the ferry timetable: if the warehouse emptied at six, the witness was still mid-river at the moment he claims he watched it happen.
A rebuttal answers a specific claim and sets out to take it apart with reasons or evidence.
Direction separates it from a polemic, which attacks a standing position uninvited — a rebuttal is always a reply.
And a bare 'that's false' is not yet a rebuttal; the form demands grounds.
Rebuttal belongs to structured argument — courtrooms, debate rounds, letters answering letters.
A quick jab in conversation is a retort; proof that ends the matter is a refutation; and when the attack arrives uninvited rather than in reply, you are reading a polemic.

In 1998 a best-selling history claimed that the ferry crews of Gull Point had abandoned their run during the great storm.
The claim stood for six years, until the town archivist Elena Voss answered it in the same journal that had praised the book.
Her reply was a rebuttal in the full sense: she matched the book claim for claim, producing the harbor log, three crew diaries, and the storm-night manifest.
She did not merely say the author was wrong.
She showed, entry by entry, that the ferries ran until the harbor itself closed.
The author conceded in the next issue — two sentences, no evidence, and, Voss noted dryly, no apology.
